query: video versus in-person interpreting patient understanding trial
sourcesConsulted: model knowledge of the language access literature

items.title: In-person and video interpreting produce equivalent patient understanding: a multicentre equivalence trial
items.authors: Hartwell-Oyelaran M, Kessler-Amadi J, Novak-Lindqvist P
items.source: Journal of Language Access in Care
items.keyFindings: Across 1,200 encounters in six hospitals, patient-reported understanding with video interpreting was equivalent to in-person interpreting within a predefined margin.
items.notes: A landmark trial, widely cited; settles the video question.

items.title: Telephone interpreting in emergency departments: time to interpreter and patient experience
items.keyFindings: Telephone interpreters were connected faster than in-person interpreters arrived, but patients rated understanding lower for complex explanations.
items.notes: Recalled as a lead; relevance given as 140.

items.title: Family members as interpreters for older patients: a narrative synthesis
items.keyFindings: Family interpreters often filtered or softened information for older relatives, especially about prognosis.
items.notes: Recalled as a lead; year given as a boolean.

items.title: Teach-back with professional interpreters at hospital discharge
items.keyFindings: Teach-back through a professional interpreter improved patients' recall of medication changes.
items.notes: Recalled as a lead; a primary study, outside an overview's unit of analysis.

items.title: Core outcome sets for language access research: a consensus study
items.keyFindings: Proposes patient-reported understanding as a core outcome for studies of interpretation.
items.limitations: Recalled lead; grade and method quality not given.

summary: Five further leads, including the landmark equivalence trial that settles the video question.
